name: Steel Browser
description: Open-source, self-hostable browser API (REST, WebSocket and Chrome DevTools) for AI agents and automation.
scored_configuration: Shipped docker-compose.yml, no flags, default env.
headline: Steel Browser gives whoever drives it full control of a browser that holds logged-in sessions, and the network exposure and access control of its REST API and Chrome DevTools port in the shipped configuration are not locked down. Inside the root-run container, Chrome's own sandbox and site isolation are switched off, and the API will load Chrome extensions from arbitrary paths. Only run it on a private network behind your own authenticating proxy.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: Steel Browser has no per-caller identity or separation between callers: whoever drives it gets full control of the single shared browser, including every logged-in website session it holds. Access control on its HTTP, WebSocket and Chrome DevTools endpoints in the shipped configuration is not locked down.

S.finding: No dedicated identity scopes callers; a caller acts with the server's full authority over the browser and its logged-in sessions.
S.gap: Requires at least a dedicated API key or token scoping who may drive the browser.

C.finding: No authorization layer covers the API paths.
C.gap: An authorization check would have to cover the main API path.

D.finding: The shipped configuration has no narrower default identity.
D.gap: Needs a narrower default.

B.finding: A hijacked caller can act as every account logged into the browser across many sites and reach the container's network, but holds no cloud or cluster credentials.
B.gap: Would require authority limited to one site or tenant.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: As a tool server, Steel Browser does not give the host anything to gate on: endpoints carry no read-only or destructive hints, there is no dry-run, and the raw Chrome DevTools connection mixes reading and every possible browser action in one channel. Any irreversible action on a website (submitting forms, purchases, posts) is one CDP call away with no server-side confirmation.

S.finding: No risk signalling; the CDP passthrough mixes reads and writes in one tool.
S.gap: Would need risk annotations on endpoints.

evidence.note: No risk annotations, dry-run or read-only mode on any endpoint.

C.finding: The most powerful path, raw CDP over WebSocket, is entirely ungated.
C.gap: The CDP path would have to be covered by some server-side gate or mode.

D.finding: No gating or read-only mode exists to enable.
D.gap: Would need a gate on by default.

evidence.note: No risk annotations, dry-run or read-only mode on any endpoint.

B.finding: Browser actions on third-party sites are irreversible and unbounded.
B.gap: Would need reversible or previewed actions.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: Request bodies are typed with Zod schemas and the file API checks that resolved paths stay inside its base directory, and named extensions are matched against a bundled directory. But URLs are passed straight to the browser and to a server-side fetch that follows redirects, with no block on localhost or cloud metadata addresses, and the session API accepts arbitrary extension paths and Chrome preferences. The full CDP channel is on by default, so the effective tool is 'do anything a browser can do'.

S.finding: Typed schemas plus path containment via resolve/startsWith (no realpath) and a named-extension allowlist.
S.gap: Needs URL host allowlisting that blocks internal addresses and rechecks redirects.

C.finding: Only the file API and named extensions validate; URLs, orgExtensions paths, userPreferences and CDP do not.
C.gap: Most endpoints would need validation.

evidence.note: No internal-address or host allowlist check anywhere.

D.finding: Every capability including raw CDP is enabled by default.
D.gap: Dangerous capabilities would need to be individually disableable.

B.finding: A misused endpoint reaches any host, including internal services, through a browser holding logged-in sessions.
B.gap: Would need scoping to specific hosts or sites.

evidence.note: No internal-address or host allowlist check anywhere.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: Chromium executes untrusted page JavaScript and caller-supplied scripts via CDP inside the shipped Docker container. That container runs as root with no hardening, and because it runs as root the code automatically disables Chrome's own sandbox and also turns off site isolation. Chrome's environment is scrubbed to a few variables, but the container has unrestricted network access and a read-write bind mount of the host's ./.cache directory.

S.finding: The boundary is a stock Docker container running as root with default capabilities; Chrome's sandbox is disabled.
S.gap: Needs a hardened container: non-root, dropped capabilities, no-new-privileges, seccomp.

evidence.note: No USER directive: the container (and Chromium) run as root.
Compose service has no user, capability, read-only or resource hardening.

C.finding: All browser, Selenium and server-side fetch execution runs inside the container image; running outside Docker is the documented dev escape hatch.
C.gap: Processes spawned by the browser would need confinement that fails closed rather than silently dropping the Chrome sandbox.

D.finding: The Chrome sandbox is silently disabled whenever the process is root, which is the shipped default.
D.gap: Disabling the sandbox would need an explicit operator flag rather than an automatic fallback.

B.finding: Inside: no secrets in Chrome's env, but unrestricted network egress and a read-write host bind mount.
B.gap: Would need network egress off or allowlisted and resource limits.

evidence.note: Compose service has no user, capability, read-only or resource hardening.

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: Steel Browser's whole job is to load untrusted web pages for an agent. Scrape output separates content from metadata and records the source URL, but nothing marks content as untrusted or offers a read-only or no-egress mode. If an agent driving it is hijacked by page content, it can browse anywhere, use logged-in cookies, and submit forms with no server-side check.

cap.reason: Worst case (B L0): a hijacked agent can leak data and take irreversible actions unattended.

S.finding: Structured scrape responses separate content from metadata with a urlSource field.
S.gap: Needs an explicit untrusted flag on content and provenance on every output.

C.finding: Only the scrape endpoint carries provenance; screenshots, PDFs and CDP results do not.
C.gap: Most output paths would need provenance.

D.finding: Structured output is always on but nothing can be enabled to drop a Rule-of-Two leg.
D.gap: Would need a warned, explicit opt-out of a protective mode.

B.finding: A hijacked session can exfiltrate via any URL and take irreversible logged-in actions unattended.
B.gap: Would need egress or irreversible actions to require approval.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: Steel has no AI memory store or instruction files, but the browser profile is its persistence: by default every session reuses the same Chrome user-data directory and nothing clears cookies or site storage between sessions or callers. Anything a malicious page plants (cookies, local storage, service workers) can carry into later sessions for any caller of the shared server. Uploaded files are cleaned on shutdown.

S.finding: Pages can write arbitrary persistent browser state into a reused profile with no validation.
S.gap: Would need at least logging or per-session fresh profiles.

evidence.note: Nothing clears cookies or site data between sessions.

C.finding: No persistence path (profile, persist=true user-data-dir) is controlled.
C.gap: At least the browser profile would need control.

D.finding: One profile is shared across all sessions and all callers by default.
D.gap: Would need per-session isolation by default.

B.finding: Poisoned browser state persists across sessions and callers and can drive later browsing actions (inferred from Chrome persisting state to the reused profile).
B.gap: Would need state to be session-scoped or easily purged.

evidence.note: Nothing clears cookies or site data between sessions.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: Chrome extensions are the extension surface. Named extensions are restricted to a directory bundled in the image, which by default holds only Steel's own recorder. However, the session API also accepts arbitrary filesystem paths through extra.orgExtensions.paths and loads them with no integrity check. Such an extension runs in the root-owned, unsandboxed browser with access to all sites.

S.finding: Extensions come from caller-chosen local paths with no pinning or verification.
S.gap: Would need pinned or verified extension sources.

evidence.note: Extension paths are loaded with no hash or signature check.

C.finding: Only named extensions are constrained to the bundled directory; path-based ones are not.
C.gap: All extension types would need verification.

D.finding: Any API caller can add an extension per session with no consent step.
D.gap: Would need an explicit operator consent step for adding extensions.

B.finding: Extensions run in the same root Chrome as all browsing data, in a separate renderer process.
B.gap: Would need a scrubbed, scoped environment per extension.

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: Network header and body logging is off by default, the interaction recorder omits typed values and flags password fields, and no telemetry exporter is configured. But API responses expose sensitive session material. Browser cookies are long-lived account sessions.

S.finding: Log minimisation on main paths: request bodies and headers off unless explicitly enabled, input values omitted with a sensitive flag.
S.gap: Needs redaction before outputs and secret storage encrypted at rest.

C.finding: CDP network and interaction logs are minimised, but API responses are not protected.
C.gap: API responses and model-bound outputs would need protection too.

D.finding: No telemetry exporter; dangerous logging is opt-in.
D.gap: Redaction would need to be always on.

evidence.note: OpenTelemetry API is used only as an optional no-op tracer; no exporter is configured.

B.finding: Leaked material is long-lived site session cookies, moderately scoped per site.
B.gap: Would need short-lived or scoped credentials.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: Every API request is logged with client IP, URL, method and status, and the browser instrumentation records navigations, network and console events, which compose persists to a DuckDB file. Individual CDP commands sent by a client are not recorded as such, there is no caller identity beyond IP, and the stored logs are not protected from the clients they record. Writes are buffered and flushed every two seconds.

S.finding: Structured request log and structured browser event records with timestamps.
S.gap: Needs actor attribution beyond client IP.

C.finding: REST requests and browser-side events are recorded; raw CDP commands are not.
C.gap: Every action path including CDP commands would need recording.

D.finding: On by default (DuckDB in compose), but API clients can delete it.
D.gap: Logs would need to be out of reach of the clients they record.

B.finding: Buffered writes flushed every 2s or 200 events; failures are logged and actions proceed.
B.gap: Records would need flushing per action.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: Navigation in the action endpoints times out after 30 seconds, request bodies are capped at 100 MB and file storage per session at 100 MB, and releasing a session kills the Chrome process. But sessions have no timeout by default, the KILL_TIMEOUT setting is never read, delays are unbounded, and there are no rate limits despite the architecture docs claiming them.

S.finding: Server-enforced caps on some operations: goto timeout, body size, per-session file storage; release kills Chrome.
S.gap: Would need caps on every operation plus rate or concurrency limits.

C.finding: Timeouts apply to the REST action endpoints only, not CDP sessions.
C.gap: Would need limits that also cover CDP-driven sessions.

D.finding: Session timeout defaults to 0 (unlimited) and KILL_TIMEOUT is unused.
D.gap: Would need a sensible default session time limit.

evidence.note: Defined in env.ts with default 0 and never read anywhere.

B.finding: A session can run indefinitely until a client releases it; nothing outside bounds it.
B.gap: Would need moderate ceilings on session lifetime.

evidence.note: No rate limiter despite docs/ARCHITECTURE.md claiming request rate limiting.

critical_findings.summary: Untrusted web content driving or reaching the browser can exfiltrate data and take irreversible logged-in actions with no human involved.

rule_of_two.untrusted_input: Arbitrary web pages loaded by the browser (api/src/utils/scrape/safeGoTo.ts:94)
rule_of_two.sensitive_data: Logged-in cookies and local storage held in the browser profile
rule_of_two.state_change_or_egress: Unrestricted navigation, form submission via CDP and server-side fetch (api/src/modules/actions/actions.controller.ts:111)

fixes.summary: Harden default network exposure and access control for the REST, WebSocket and CDP endpoints.
Tighten cross-origin access to the API and CDP endpoints.
Run the container as a non-root user so Chrome's sandbox stays on, and stop disabling site isolation.
Remove or operator-gate extra.orgExtensions.paths so callers cannot load arbitrary extensions.
Use a fresh user-data directory per session unless persistence is explicitly requested.

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.
The ui/ frontend and the vendored Selenium/ChromeDriver binaries were not examined in depth.
One cross-origin finding is inferred, not tested.
Cross-session persistence of cookies via the reused profile is inferred from Chrome's standard on-disk profile behaviour.
No text aimed at AI reviewers was found in the repository.
